He was born in 1914 on a sharecropper's cotton patch in Alabama and was as country-poor as it is possible to be. In theory the farm was - it had been rented as - a cotton and vegetable farm. But the vegetables did not feed the family, not by the time Joe, the seventh child, came along. His father broke, as sharecroppers do, from the daily strain of not making enough in crops either to feed his children or put shoes on them. They had no money to send him to a hospital. So he was carried off to a state institution where he died. A widower cam to help out and soon married Joe's mother. And his five children moved in with the eight Louises. Joe got a little more food and went to a one-room school. Then the family moved to Detroit, where the stepfather worked in an automobile factory. Joe went on to trade school and worked in the evenings doing the rounds with an ice-wagon. Then came the Depression, and the family went on relief. This, said Joe, made his mother feel very bad. Years later Joe wrote out a careful cheque for $269, which was the amount of the relief cheques they had had from the government. That, said Joe, made Mrs Brooks, as she now was, feel better.

Source: Cooke, Alistair. Letter From America (p. 20-21), original broadcast on March 18, 1949. Alfred A Knopf.

The Barrel of all 1919's are a separate item. You can change them in the field. You just screw them in. They have a spring detente if I recall. You have a head spacing go/not gauge that you place between the bolt face and the barrel as you screw it in. Most old hand just screwed it in until it would not go into battery and backed it off two clicks. Unlike most modern machine guns the M1919 had a pawl and cam the pulled the round out of the belt and slid it down the T slot in the face of the bolt. The spring loaded pawl would disengage from the round when the bullet had entered the chamber. The spent round would either fall out of the T slot of the bolt face when the mouth cleared the barrel or it could be pushed out by the new round being positioned in the chamber. Rimmed cases probably worked better than rimless cases even though there wasn't any problems with rimless ammo as far as I know. By the M1919 still lives on in the famous M2 Browing 50 cal machine gun. The are the same except the .50 is a lot bigger and heavier.
